site.title: things i've built
site.tagline: AI in commercial operations, and at home
site.name: Andy Keeley

intro:
I'm a commercial leader, not a developer. In February I started building with Claude Code, on the view that the tools had quietly become good enough for someone who understands the problem to build the fix themselves. Seven months on, it's how I prepare for negotiations, answer RFPs, keep the CRM honest and run my week. The hard part was never the code. It was describing the problem properly, arguing with the output until it was right, and then actually using it.

At home, my kids have worked out that if they can describe it, we can build it.

work.title: at work
work.framing: Commercial problems first. The technology is whatever got the job done.
work.key: effort = how long it took to build · value = what it's worth to me · usage = how often it's used

home.title: at home
home.framing: Mostly built because someone at home asked for it.

projects.name: mentor-agent
projects.strapline: A chief of staff with an IQ of 140, sitting on my shoulder.
bullets: Reads my calendar and inbox every morning and tells me what actually matters today, not just what's loudest
Runs my GTD system and EOS rocks, and holds me to account when something slips
Captures every loose end, and keeps track of what I'm still waiting on from other people
Prepares me for every negotiation with a structured six-part deal prep
Second pair of eyes on contracts and addenda, clause by clause, before they go to the lawyers
Writes the briefs that get outstanding results out of Claude Design
projects.outcome: Nothing gets dropped, and every hard conversation starts prepared.

value.tip: genuinely can't work without it now

projects.name: rfp builder
projects.strapline: Every RFP answer drafted from what we've actually said and delivered before, so the week goes on the win strategy.
bullets: Builds one corpus from past proposals, RFI answers, product documents and the security questionnaire
Drafts each answer from that corpus, and lists the sources it used
Marks every question direct, partial or gap, and leaves the gaps blank for a human to write properly
projects.outcome: More consistent answers, and the time goes into the ones that win the bid, not retyping the ones we've written twenty times.

effort.tip: two months of tuning on a real bid

value.tip: the first draft stops being the hard part

projects.name: deal prep
projects.strapline: Six questions answered before every negotiation, every time.
bullets: A questioning agent that won't produce anything until it has the value case, the narrative, the facts to hand, the leverage, the likely objections and the ask
Produces a one-page brief to take into the room
Three levels of challenge, from guiding to radical candour, depending on what's at stake
projects.outcome: No negotiation starts on instinct alone.

effort.tip: rewritten every time a negotiation taught me something

value.tip: i walk in knowing my walk-away

projects.name: customer-health-dashboard
projects.strapline: Every customer's health on one page, straight into the board pack.
bullets: Reads the customer hub exports and aged debt reports
Weights them into a single health score across the whole customer portfolio
Renders a dashboard that goes straight into the board pack
projects.outcome: Replaced a manual process that used to eat an afternoon.

projects.name: deal sprint board
projects.strapline: Every open deal, its stage and whether we're genuinely ready to close, on one screen.
bullets: One board across every deal in the quarter's sprint
Each deal shows five gates (committed, proven, priced, timed, clear) plus a readiness spine drawn from its deal prep
Readiness is calculated from the gaps, never hand-set, so it can't go stale
projects.outcome: The pipeline conversation starts from evidence, not optimism.

effort.tip: started as one html file, grew a server

value.tip: hard to argue with a red gate

usage.tip: the length of one quarter's sprint

projects.name: hotel booking engine
projects.strapline: A working booking journey on our own hotel API, built to show engineering what was possible.
bullets: Search, results, rooms, basket and book, end to end
Built on our own Universal Hotel API, not a mock
My first real build, made to start a conversation with the engineering team
projects.outcome: Their reaction was the whole point.

effort.tip: my first real build, steep learning curve

value.tip: proved the concept to the team

projects.name: hubspot integration
projects.strapline: The CRM kept in line with the real pipeline, without the Friday-afternoon admin.
bullets: Pulled open deals from HubSpot and reconciled them against the working pipeline
Pushed changes back with a dry run first, so nothing moved in the CRM without being seen
A separate verification check to prove a deal had landed as intended
projects.outcome: Retired when the book got small enough to manage directly.

effort.tip: a few scripts and a lot of field mapping

value.tip: killed the friday-afternoon admin while it lasted

projects.name: sorry-quick-q
projects.strapline: The answer to "what kit does he need on Thursday?" at 7am, without asking the group chat.
projects.description: A knowledge base built from the boys' school comms — letters, newsletters, WhatsApp forwards, photos of a noticeboard — answering "what kit does he need Thursday?" at 7am, instead of asking the group chat. School comms constantly overwrite themselves, so nothing is ever deleted: new facts supersede old ones, but only if the source outranks what it replaces — a parent's forward can't retire the school's own letter. Citations resolve by ID so the model can't invent a source, and "I don't know" is a first-class answer.

effort.tip: two repos, and a week of arguing about supersession

value.tip: answers it before i have to ask the group chat

projects.name: investment-agent
projects.strapline: A trading agent with rules it can't talk itself out of, running on real money.
projects.description: Autonomous trading agent. Scans the crypto market, scores candidates on momentum, sentiment, risk/reward and liquidity, sizes the position through a risk manager, executes on Kraken, and emails me a daily digest of what it did and why. The interesting part isn't the trading — it's the rules it can't talk itself out of: stop-loss set at entry, a hard cash floor, a maximum hold it has to re-underwrite. Runs unattended.

effort.tip: weekends and evenings over ~3 weeks, still tuning

projects.name: zenbox
projects.strapline: A quiet inbox on rules I control, which replaced a paid subscription.
projects.description: Self-hosted email triage that replaced a paid SaneBox subscription. Gmail pushes new mail through Pub/Sub to a service that sorts it on rules I control — whitelist, greylist, am-I-actually-a-recipient, bulk-mail detection. Two independent instances, one per mailbox, sharing only the code. Plus a Chrome extension so I can change a sender's rule without leaving the inbox.

value.tip: cancelled the subscription, kept the quiet inbox

projects.name: fitness-mentor
projects.strapline: A training coach that checks my own data before it tells me anything.
projects.description: My coach. Knows my training history, my weak points and every session I've logged. Five modes — log, review, plan, check, rehab. The bit I'm proudest of: before it does anything else it runs the arithmetic on my own data and tells me what's drifted — a skipped session, a stale flag, rehab that isn't going in, or a training block that quietly finished two weeks ago and I hadn't noticed. There's a phone app for logging sets at the rack, and it wrote the brief I took to my physio.

effort.tip: restructured twice as i worked out what i needed

value.tip: replaced a coach i was paying for

projects.name: health-tracker
projects.strapline: What I drink, set against what my heart rate and sleep make of it.
projects.description: Correlates what I drink with what my body does about it — resting heart rate, HRV and sleep score, straight from Garmin. Dose-response curves, streak analysis, and the uncomfortable chart where the trend line meets the weekend. Guilt-as-a-service.

projects.name: maths-challenge
projects.strapline: Maths practice for two nine-year-olds, disguised as a fighting game.
projects.description: Maths practice for my boys, disguised as a fighting game. Eight Key Stage 2 topics; each round is a match against an opponent with a health bar, a super meter that rewards streaks, and a rank stamp at the end. Nothing in it reads as losing — that was a design rule. There's a second area of trials modelled on their school's cognitive assessment. The save file has no reset button, on purpose: their history is the only record of what they've played, and the only input for tuning the difficulty.

effort.tip: the most iterated thing i've built

projects.name: anki-srs
projects.strapline: Spaced repetition built properly, for paintings, capitals and commercial fundamentals.
projects.description: Spaced repetition built properly — SM-2 scheduling, four-button grading, and an append-only review log so I can swap the algorithm out later without losing history. Card types are pluggable, so one deck of famous paintings became decks for capitals, flags, US states, life philosophies and commercial fundamentals.

effort.tip: a weekend, then kept extending it

value.tip: the commercial deck earns its keep

projects.name: sonic-fighters
projects.strapline: A 3D browser fighting game, rebuilt once they kept asking for more characters.
projects.description: A browser fighting game for my boys. Three.js, a physically-based rendering pipeline, a night arena and a broadcast-style HUD. Started as a weekend thing, then got rebuilt from the visuals up once they kept asking for more characters.

effort.tip: rebuilt once i knew what good looked like

projects.name: realm-raiders
projects.strapline: A split-screen co-op adventure for two players on one laptop.
projects.description: Split-screen 3D co-op adventure for two players on one laptop. Procedural low-poly island, camera-relative movement, terrain and obstacle collision, character abilities. Built in phases from a written spec — walking skeleton first, structured so combat and characters bolt on cleanly afterwards.

usage.tip: when we get a rainy afternoon

projects.name: beyblade-clash
projects.strapline: A Beyblade battle in the browser, built in an evening because they asked.
projects.description: Two-to-three player Beyblade battle in the browser. Spin physics, collisions, stadium walls, hand-drawn bey art. Built in an evening because they asked.

projects.name: wordle-solver
projects.strapline: Suggests the Wordle guess that rules out the most answers.
projects.description: Wordle solver over the official NYT answer list. Feed it what you know and it suggests the guess that eliminates the most remaining possibilities. Deployed, so anyone can use it.

projects.name: fitness-tracker
projects.strapline: The first thing I ever deployed, and where I learned what deploying involves.
projects.description: Workout logger with reusable templates and a rest timer, deployed on Render with Postgres behind it. My first database-backed web app, and where I learned what deploying actually involves. Now superseded by the logging app inside fitness-mentor.

value.tip: did its job, then got replaced

closing: If you've got a problem that feels like it should be software but you don't have developers to build it — [get in touch](mailto:andy.keeley@gmail.com). I might be able to help.
